1	---
2	name: test-quality
3	description: >-
4	  What makes a test worth keeping, and the catalog of ways tests pass while
5	  proving nothing. Every test states its WHY (and CLAIM id); co-located tests;
6	  monoid laws, model-based state-machine properties, oracles, reviewed goldens,
7	  parity tests for mated interfaces; cheap manual mutation checks and periodic
8	  mutation tooling; explicit tautology hunting; plus the full failure-mode
9	  catalog with detection hints and fixes (tautology, over-mocking, asserting
10	  current behavior, happy-path only, host-timezone dependence, skipped
11	  fixtures, source-grep guards, wrong-layer pins, shared-table round trips).
12	  Use when writing tests, reviewing a test diff, fixing a red test, auditing a
13	  suite, or when a subagent (rg-implement or build-loop red phase) hands back
14	  tests. Companions: technical-excellence, build-loop.
15	---
16	
17	# Test quality
18	
19	A green run says nothing about whether a test can fail. For every test you
20	write or review, answer one question: **if the bug came back, would this go
21	red?** If you can't name the bug it catches, it's hollow.
22	
23	| Skill | Load it when |
24	|---|---|
25	| `technical-excellence` | The test proves an interface, invariant or CLAIM, or a type could make the test unnecessary. Source of the CLAIM convention and mated-part (parity) rule. |
26	| `build-loop` | You are in a red/green run or a review round. Its red gate uses this skill; review findings about tests are judged with it. |
27	
28	## 1. Every test says why
29	
30	The reason a test exists is hard to recall later. Annotate each test with a
31	short WHY: the bug, rule, incident or claim it guards.
32	
33	```
34	// why: a partial chunk must never be ACKed (invariant 3.1; regression of the
35	//      2026-09 early-ack bug). Fails if commit moves after ack.
36	// proves: CLAIM(ack-order)
37	```
38	
39	- A test proving a CLAIM (see `technical-excellence`) names its id, so the
40	  claim's grep finds its proof.
41	- No why, no keep: a test whose purpose nobody can state is a deletion
42	  candidate.
43	- Expected values show their derivation (spec section, capture, arithmetic).
44	
45	## 2. Placement
46	
47	Co-locate tests with the code they test, unless the repo's convention says
48	otherwise (when in Rome). A test beside its module shows what the abstraction
49	is, travels with it, and is deleted with it. Cross-cutting and end-to-end
50	suites live apart, and say so in their why.
51	
52	## 3. Techniques worth using
53	
54	### Monoids and accumulators
55	If a type combines (`combine`, identity element), property-test the laws:
56	
57	| Law | Property |
58	|---|---|
59	| Identity | `combine(x, empty) == x == combine(empty, x)` |
60	| Associativity | `combine(combine(a,b),c) == combine(a,combine(b,c))` |
61	| Commutativity | `combine(a,b) == combine(b,a)` (only if claimed) |
62	| Split-merge | for any split of the input, `combine(fold(left), fold(right)) == fold(whole)` (single pass equals chunked/parallel/incremental) |
63	
64	Generate inputs randomly with a fixed seed; shrink failures.
65	
66	### State machines
67	Model-based property tests: a small pure model of the intended states and
68	transitions; generate random command sequences; apply to model and real
69	system; assert observable state agrees after every step, and that illegal
70	transitions are refused. Include crash/rollback and retry commands.
71	
72	### Oracles
73	Expected values come from something independent of the code under test:
74	- a slow, obviously-correct reference implementation;
75	- a hand-computed fixture (arithmetic in a comment);
76	- a real capture or spec table, decoded field by field.
77	Beware a shared oracle: incremental-vs-forced parity can pass while both
78	paths inherit the same regression. Keep an independently derived fixture next
79	to the parity test.
80	
81	### Goldens
82	High quality means: reviewed by a person, minimal (smallest input that shows
83	the behavior), deterministic (zone, clock, seed, locale pinned), explained
84	(why: what it pins, version or pin it was generated at). Regeneration is a
85	deliberate, flagged act, never silent. A golden nobody inspected is mode 12.
86	Retain exact comparison for a fixed version; do not hide change behind a
87	blanket tolerance.
88	
89	### Parity tests for mated interfaces
90	Writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server: test both against literal
91	bytes or messages from the spec or a real capture, field by field, not just
92	against each other. Round-trip tests are a supplement, never the proof.
93	Dedupe parity corpora and report the real unique count.
94	
95	## 4. Mutation checks
96	
97	**Cheap manual mutations (do these every time).** Pick 3-5 spots in the code
98	under test, mutate one at a time, run the focused tests:
99	
100	| Mutation | If still green |
101	|---|---|
102	| Flip a condition (`<` to `<=`, `&&` to `\|\|`, negate) | Boundary or branch untested |
103	| Delete a line or a call | That line is unproven; or the test is at the wrong layer |
104	| Change a constant (offset, threshold, default) | Value not asserted exactly |
105	| Swap two arguments or an ordering | Order not pinned |
106	
107	Use the result to decide: more tests needed, or tests that prove nothing
108	(remove them). Revert every mutation; never commit one.
109	
110	**`# catches:` and post-green spot mutations (build-loop red/green).** Each
111	red test carries a `# catches: <a plausible wrong implementation this fails>`
112	line. If you cannot name one, the test is likely a tautology; rewrite or drop
113	it. After green, the orchestrator applies 2-3 of those named wrong
114	implementations and checks the matching tests go red. A green implementer that
115	edits a red test says so in its report; the edit becomes a review finding.
116	
117	**Mutation tool, periodically.** If the stack has one (for example Stryker,
118	mutmut, cargo-mutants, PIT), run it every so often on a stable module.
119	Surviving mutants show gaps. Tests that kill no unique mutant and duplicate
120	another test's kills are candidates to prune, which keeps the standard suite
121	small and fast.
122	
123	## 5. Hunt tautology explicitly
124	
125	Before approving any test, ask of each assertion: *can this expression be
126	false given any implementation?* Tautology signs: value compared to itself;
127	mock returns what it was told; expected computed by the function under test;
128	a literal's length asserted on the literal; a test of a pasted copy; a
129	mirrored formula. Mode 1 and 5 below, with fixes. For tautology, the
130	tool is the "revert the fix" mutation.
131	
132	## 6. The mutation check that catches most failure modes
133	
134	Mentally (or actually) mutate the code under test and see if the test fails:
135	
136	1. Revert the fix the test claims to pin. Still green? The test is wrong.
137	2. Delete the call site the test claims to cover (not the helper: the place
138	   production calls it). Still green? Wrong layer.
139	3. Empty the list, set or config the test iterates over. Still green? Vacuous.
140	4. Run it under `TZ=UTC` and under a DST zone. Different result, or a skip?
141	   Host-dependent.
142	5. Remove the fixture file. Skip with no CI failure? It never runs in CI.
143	
144	Before calling a suite done, do 1 for at least the tests whose names claim a
145	bug.
146	
147	## 7. Classic modes
148	
149	| # | Mode | Looks like | Fix |
150	|---|---|---|---|
151	| 1 | Tautology | Value compared to itself; mock returns what it was told; expected computed by the function under test; `hasLength(12)` on a 12-item literal; `isNotNull` on a tear-off | Expected value from the spec or a hand calculation |
152	| 2 | Over-mocking | The engine/unit under test is stubbed; only fakes run | Mock the clock, network, platform. Never the unit |
153	| 3 | Asserts current behavior | Magic numbers with no derivation (`9.03`, `closeTo(50, 8)`); comment-free goldens | Show the arithmetic in a comment, or cite the spec/capture the value came from |
154	| 4 | Happy path only | No empty, null, zero, negative, NaN, boundary, duplicate, truncated, error, or thin-input case | List the edge cases before writing the first test |
155	| 5 | Mirrored implementation | Test re-implements the formula, or tests a pasted copy of a private helper | Hand-computed constants; test the real symbol |
156	| 6 | Coverage theater | Code runs, nothing meaningful is asserted; benchmark tests with no `expect` | Every test asserts a concrete value |
157	| 7 | Existence only | `isNotNull`, `isNotEmpty`, `returnsNormally`, `greaterThan(0)`, `isA<T>()`, `verify(called)` where the exact value is known | Assert the value. If the seeded row count is 3, assert 3 |
158	| 8 | Weakened during a fix | Exact value became a range; case deleted; `skip:` added; tolerance widened | Treat any loosened test in a fix diff as a red flag. Change the code, not the test. `git log -p` the test file |
159	| 9 | Volume over quality | Dozens of near-identical cases; parity corpora where the same records repeat (978 unique of 2,934) | Fewer, distinct cases; dedupe corpora and report the real count |
160	| 10 | Confidently wrong | Expected value contradicts the spec, docs, or the test's own earlier assertion | Flag uncertain inputs instead of guessing |
161	| 11 | Unreadable failure | `expect(cond, isTrue)` with no `reason:`; byte lists without hex | Match on the value, or add `reason:` naming expected vs actual |
162	| 12 | Blind golden | Snapshot regenerated by an env var; nobody inspected it | Golden only reviewed output; note who checked it and against what |
163	
164	## 8. Modes the classic list misses
165	
166	These came up across three repos, often in tests that looked careful.
167	
168	**Host-timezone dependence.** DST and local-vs-UTC tests that only bite when
169	the machine's zone differs from UTC, or that `markTestSkipped` unless
170	`TZ == America/Denver`. CI runners are UTC, so the check is vacuous there.
171	Calls that default to the host zone (no offset argument) also flip results
172	by zone. Fix: pin the zone inside the test, or pass the offset explicitly.
173	Never derive the expected value with the same `toLocal()` the code uses.
174	Run CI as a matrix: UTC plus one DST zone.
175	
176	**Silently skipped fixtures.** The test skips when a data file is absent,
177	and that file is gitignored or lives outside the repo. CI never runs it, yet
178	it's often the only end-to-end or real-capture test. Fix: commit a small
179	fixture, or make the skip loud in CI (fail when `CI` is set). Same for sibling
180	checkouts: a guard that skips unless `../analytics` exists, when the real
181	directory is `../openstrap-analytics`, has never run anywhere. Golden groups
182	that skip because the golden directory is absent are the same mode.
183	
184	**Source-grep guards.** "Ordering is untouched" checks that two identifiers
185	appear in a file; "prune order" checks `indexOf` positions; a "no 86400 s"
186	guard covers 22 hand-listed files and misses `86_400`. These pass if a comment
187	contains the string, if the code is reordered in a way the regex can't see,
188	or if the bug lands in an unlisted file. Fix: drive the behavior (seed a
189	partial day, prune, assert rows survive). Keep grep guards only as a backstop,
190	cover the whole tree, and include a positive control proving the pattern
191	matches something. A whole-tree scan for a new caller or forbidden dependency
192	is the legitimate kind (an audit of 88 guard files kept 18 of this type,
193	converted 48 to behavior tests, and removed 22).
194	
195	**Pins dead code or the wrong layer.** The test exercises a pure helper, but
196	production reads the value through a different path. Real examples: a
197	readiness-flash test pinning a getter with zero callers; a freeze test that
198	covers the pure function but not where the screen reads or the engine writes;
199	a race test that never imports the service and tests `List.remove`; an "edge
200	half" test that only calls the sibling library; "the stager only runs inside
201	`Isolate.run`" checked by two strings anywhere in the file (output parity is
202	not execution placement). Fix: test through the seam the user hits, or add a
203	test that the production path calls the helper.
204	
205	**Shared-table round trip.** The test builds a frame at offset 13 and the
206	parser reads offset 13 from the same constant. A wrong offset passes. Fix:
207	literal bytes from a real capture or the spec, decoded field by field. When a
208	real capture exists, assert every field you can hand-decode, not just the
209	version byte or the first 4 of 8 token bytes.
210	
211	**Capability tested once, wired N times.** The new decoder is tested
212	directly, but two other entry points still call the old one. Fix: count the
213	entry points and test each, or add a guard that they all route through one.
214	
215	**Iterating over the current set.** `for (op in dangerousCmds) expect(...)`
216	stays green when the set is emptied or an item is dropped. Fix: pin the
217	required members by name, then loop.
218	
219	**Conditional assertions.** `if (row != null) expect(...)` passes with nothing
220	checked. Fix: assert the precondition first.
221	
222	**Assertions on absence with no positive control.** "Nothing was written"
223	checked via `total_changes` or a log line, without proving the probe moves on
224	a real write. A no-bounce check that matches log wording passes if the log is
225	reworded. Fix: show the probe detects the positive case in the same test.
226	
227	**Test-only configuration.** The test runs with thresholds (300/200/200) that
228	differ from shipped defaults (200/150/750). Fix: test the shipped defaults,
229	plus overrides as separate cases.
230	
231	**Change-detector literals.** `expect(kAlgoVersion, 104)` or a literal SHA.
232	It fails on every bump and catches nothing. Fix: assert the property you care
233	about (the pinned commit contains the cited change).
234	
235	**Real time.** `DateTime.now()`, real `Future.delayed` sleeps, and "nothing
236	yet" checked after 300 ms. Flaky near midnight and on slow runners; a real
237	one-minute wait inside a correctness test costs a minute on every run. Fix:
238	`fakeAsync` with `withClock`, or inject the clock.
239	
240	**Tolerance that spans the plausible universe.** VO2max accepted in 30-70
241	when the hand value is 49.14; RMSSD up to 500 ms; one-sided bounds with no
242	upper limit; `closeTo(50, 8)` where the formula gives exactly 50 at z=0, so
243	weights and signs go untested. Fix: tolerance sized to numeric error, not to
244	"looks reasonable."
245	
246	## 9. Domain checks worth adding wherever they apply
247	
248	- **Absent input.** Missing or thin input returns null, absent, or "—", never
249	  a default or a value derived from another metric.
250	- **Idempotence.** Run the computation three times with slightly more data;
251	  the persisted value stays stable. Append a duplicate day; the baseline
252	  doesn't move.
253	- **Failure paths.** Every flag set on the happy path is cleared on error,
254	  timeout, and give-up.
255	- **Durability ordering.** Commit before acknowledge, tested by driving the
256	  real engine and observing the order, including a rollback case.
257	- **Ambient state.** Globals that change output are re-armed inside isolate
258	  closures, and a test shows output changes when they're set.
259	
260	## 10. Grounding from suite audits
261	
262	Two audits of a large suite (about 14,000 test blocks across three repos)
263	produced these lessons; use them to prioritize.
264	
265	| Lesson | What to do |
266	|---|---|
267	| Many tests never ran: TZ-gated, fixture-gated, sibling-checkout-gated skips | Fix execution first (TZ matrix, committed fixtures, fail-on-skip under `CI`) before writing new tests. |
268	| Invariant gaps sat next to thousands of passing tests (ACK ordering, prune safety, RAM-only streams, dangerous-opcode lists) | Map each written invariant to a behavioral test that drives the real engine; grep-guards do not count. |
269	| Source-grep guards: 88 audited, about a fifth worth keeping | Keep whole-tree dependency/caller bans with a positive control; convert ordering/token greps to behavior; delete comment-proximity checks. |
270	| Shared-oracle limit: incremental-vs-forced parity passes when both inherit a regression | Keep an independent versioned fixture beside parity tests; store the generating algorithm version/pin with each golden. |
271	| Characterization suites overlap controller tests, but not fully | Trim case by case; do not delete wholesale. Check what the higher layer still uniquely covers (real claims, persistence, races). |
272	| Real waits dominated cost (a 60 s breathing session, fixed 5 s reply windows) | Inject clocks and parameterize windows; keep timing out of correctness tests. |
273	| Vacuous tolerances and `greaterThan(0)` everywhere | Sweep mechanically after reworks, not before, to avoid collisions. |
274	| A test endorsed behavior a written invariant forbids | When a test and an invariant conflict, stop and ask the owner. Do not "fix" either silently. |
275	| Golden baseline failed after an algorithm version bump; nothing recorded which version made it | Diff old vs new at field level; rebaseline only if all changes are the intended ones; store version and pin beside the golden. |
276	
277	## 11. When writing tests (especially as a subagent)
278	
279	- Write expectations from the spec before reading the implementation's
280	  output. Show the arithmetic.
281	- State each test's why and CLAIM id (section 1).
282	- List inputs you're unsure about instead of inventing expected values.
283	- Confirm each new test fails against the broken code (red first).
284	- Never loosen an existing assertion to make a fix pass. If it must change,
285	  say why in the commit message.
286	
287	## 12. When reviewing
288	
289	Read assertions before the green checkmark. For each test, name the bug it
290	catches and run the mutation check above. Report hollow tests with the
291	assertion quoted, the mode, and a concrete fix.

1	---
2	name: technical-excellence
3	description: >-
4	  Design and code standards for work that must stay correct: rich interfaces
5	  (errors, reason, invariants, parity tests), cited claims with grep-able ids,
6	  deep modules, a project lexicon with disciplined naming, type-level safety
7	  (invalid states unrepresentable, monoids, exhaustive matching), and a
8	  threat-model check on security. Use when designing an abstraction, writing or
9	  reviewing code or comments, naming things, or judging a review finding.
10	  Companions: test-quality (proving it), build-loop (the workflow).
11	---
12	
13	# technical-excellence
14	
15	Standards for what the code says and how it is shaped.
16	
17	| Skill | Load it when |
18	|---|---|
19	| `test-quality` | Writing or reviewing the tests that prove an interface, claim or invariant here. |
20	| `build-loop` | The work is multi-phase, or a cross-model review will judge it. Its review step uses sections 6 and 7 below. |
21	
22	First rule: **when in Rome.** Follow the repo's conventions (AGENTS.md,
23	existing style, lexicon) before anything below. Apply this skill where the repo
24	is silent.
25	
26	## 1. Rich interfaces
27	
28	An interface is more than signatures. Each abstraction documents:
29	
30	| Part | Says |
31	|---|---|
32	| Error detail | What can fail, and how it is reported (type, code, null, exception). Callers must be able to handle each case without reading the body. |
33	| Reason | Why it exists. What breaks or duplicates if it is removed. |
34	| Invariants | What is always true before, during and after calls. |
35	| Mating parts | If it has a second or third counterpart (writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server), name them. |
36	
37	**Mated parts need parity tests** proving both sides agree: round trip, plus
38	independent fixtures (see `test-quality`, parity and oracles). A pair that is
39	only tested against each other's constants proves nothing.
40	
41	## 2. Claims are cited
42	
43	Module-level comments and comments above code blocks contain verifiable
44	claims ("this is O(n)", "the device sends big-endian", "idempotent",
45	"commit happens before ACK"). Every such claim is anchored and sourced.
46	
47	Convention (adapt the comment syntax to the language):
48	
49	```
50	// CLAIM(ack-order): the commit completes before the ACK is sent [spec §4.2; ack_order_test]
51	...
52	// ↳ CLAIM(ack-order)
53	ack(token);
54	```
55	
56	- The comment states a **verifiable** claim and its **source or proof** in
57	  brackets: a spec section, capture file, proof sketch, or test name.
58	- The code the claim governs carries `↳ CLAIM(<id>)`.
59	- A maintainer changing that code greps the id, finds the claim and its
60	  proof, and re-checks it.
61	- Tests that prove the claim name the id in their why (`test-quality`).
62	- Ids are short, unique, stable. Unprovable "claims" are opinions: label them
63	  as such or delete them. A comment with no source is a rumor.
64	
65	## 3. Deep modules
66	
67	Prefer a simple interface over a substantial implementation. Few entry
68	points, few parameters, no leaked internals. Smells: shallow wrappers that
69	forward one call; interfaces as long as the body; callers that must know
70	call order. Hide the complexity; do not spread it across callers.
71	
72	## 4. Lexicon and naming
73	
74	Keep a project lexicon (a glossary doc: term, meaning, where it lives). Name
75	code in correspondence with it. Add a term to the glossary when you coin one;
76	do not use two words for one concept.
77	
78	Outside any convention:
79	
80	- Clear names, **no abbreviations**.
81	- 1-2 primary words, plus optional small words (determiners, prepositions):
82	  `rowsToPrune`, `nightOfRecord`.
83	- Be deliberate about grammar:
84	  - functions and methods: verbs (`parseFrame`); predicates read as
85	    questions (`isFinalized`, `hasPendingWrite`);
86	  - values and types: nouns (`dayLabel`, `HistoryToken`);
87	  - qualifiers: adjectives (`pendingRows`);
88	  - tense shows state: `committedRows` (done), `rowsToCommit` (not yet).
89	- Name by how the value is used, not its type. Avoid vague names such as
90	  `value`, `data`, `result`, `tmp`. A function that sums two numbers returns
91	  `sum`; a truly generic result is `returnValue`.
92	
93	## 5. Type-level safety first
94	
95	Algorithmic and algebraic design shrinks runtime checks, tests and review.
96	Reach for these before adding a check:
97	
98	| Tool | Effect |
99	|---|---|
100	| Make invalid states unrepresentable (sum types, non-empty lists, state enums carrying only valid fields) | The bug cannot compile. No test or review needed. |
101	| Newtypes / branded types (`LocalDayLabel` vs `UtcTimestamp`, `Milliseconds` vs `Seconds`) | Mixed-up units and ids fail to compile. |
102	| Exhaustive matching, no default branch | Adding a case forces every consumer to be updated. |
103	| Monoids (identity, associative combine) for accumulators | Split-merge equals single pass; parallelism and incrementality are safe. Prove laws with property tests (`test-quality`). |
104	| Parse, don't validate: convert raw input to a checked type once, at the boundary | Inner code never re-checks. |
105	| Smart constructors, private fields | Invariants hold by construction. |
106

1	# Notification flow pilot
2	
3	## Intent and scope
4	
5	Make the owner's notification categories, schedules, and budgets responsive and reliable on the existing `rework` pilot. Preserve explicit cancellation, spend only on actual delivery, default to recent notifications, add automation, and replace the window editor with a focused timeline. Snoozing and original-source icons are opt-in experiments, each independently disableable. No upstream publication or broad reskin is included.
6	
7	Base: `8b7c2ece17344402737dd7b567f7e139df8f826a`. This branch is itself a pilot, as explicitly requested by the owner on 2026-11-17. Retain it as a reference if a later structural implementation starts fresh. Earlier audit and diagnostic tooling are part of the preparation checkpoint.
8	
9	## Owner decisions
10	
11	- Only explicit notification cancellation clears queued notifications. Opening an app alone does not.
12	- Cleared before delivery costs zero. Clearing a delivered notification does not refund spending.
13	- Notification priority precedes per-app queue preference. App queue preference cannot override it.
14	- Newest first is the default; apps may opt into oldest first and a higher position within the same notification priority.
15	- Retain distinct older notifications. Updates to a pending notification replace its contents and move it according to its updated recency.
16	- Optimize both category/app management and the inbox/dashboard, including scrolling.
17	- Schedule intents choose repeating or dated mode. Omitted mode defaults to repeating.
18	- Budget/window edits preserve spending already incurred. Spent 6, new budget 10 means 4 remaining.
19	- Manual and automated edits use last change wins.
20	- Windows continuously cover the entire local day, with shared boundaries and a one-hour minimum.
21	- A newly split window goes immediately after the focused window. Two adjacent 90-minute windows can become three adjacent one-hour windows, including borrowing from the preceding neighbor when the focused window is the latter.
22	- Failure to find enough time shows an error dialog with instructions for enlarging suitable windows.
23	- Preserve Edge's fast drag, hold for minute precision, and zoom controls.
24	
25	## Delivery and cancellation contract
26	
27	One coordinator must serialize arrival, explicit clearing, and scheduled delivery decisions. Recheck pending state at authorization; a stale batch snapshot must not resurrect a cleared row. Preserve cancellation information when asynchronous arrival processing would otherwise overwrite a newer removal. Farhan's own interception/snoozing removal is not an explicit source-app cancellation. Distinguish removal reasons.
28	
29	Budget spending and delivered state must remain consistent across overlapping immediate/batch attempts and repeated callbacks. A notification key already delivered must not spend again solely because its contents update. Define the durable decision and notification-post failure boundary explicitly; notification manager effects cannot participate in a Room transaction. Do not advertise exactly-once delivery across a crash without evidence. On a posting failure, do not report a successful delivery or permanently lose its budget allowance.
30	
31	Queue order: notification priority, per-app queue rank, then candidate recency. Within a priority/rank group, choose the head of each app's queue according to that app's newest/oldest policy; compare eligible heads by recency with deterministic ties. A configurable FIFO app must not bypass higher-priority items. Stable notification keys identify updates; timestamps alone do not identify distinct notifications.
32	
33	Bound action-store ownership and make mutations safe across service/UI coroutines. Release eligible tap/reply/proxy entries on deletion and clearing, including clear-all. Preserve queued actions needed for delivery. Avoid new background polling for cleanup or source discovery.
34	
35	## Schedule model and automation
36	
37	Represent the day as [0, 1440) minutes, displaying the final boundary as 24:00. The current 23:59 endpoint omits a minute and must migrate without losing saved budgets. Reject malformed fields, overlaps, gaps, negative budgets, and windows shorter than 60 minutes. Every entry point uses the same validator and write path. Valid changes are atomic; invalid automation leaves the saved schedule and spend unchanged.
38	
39	Repeating schedules use the phone's local wall clock. Dated overrides target one explicit ISO local date and use the repeating schedule on other dates. Last successfully accepted write wins for its applicable scope. A repeating write supersedes the currently applicable dated override so a manual edit is not silently hidden. Repeating/dated intent replay must not refill spending. Date and timezone tests use explicit clocks/zones; no 86,400-second assumption for calendar days.
40	
41	Keep an accounting identity independent of editable boundary positions. Moving, splitting, merging, or reapplying a currently active window must not manufacture a new budget allowance. Natural passage into a new window/day may reset its allowance. Specify how an accepted edit changes that transition, preserving current spending; prove with tests.
42	
43	Provide a versioned explicit Android intent contract suitable for Tasker: payload is a complete validated schedule plus mode and optional local date. Default mode is repeating. No automatic sensor integration is included. Acknowledgement/error must be observable without exposing notification content. External automation is opt-in and authenticated with a locally generated credential that the owner can copy/revoke; do not place the credential or private notification content in logs. Bound payload size and reject unknown versions. Document action, receiver, fields, date behavior, replacement behavior, examples, and validation errors from the shipped implementation.
44	
45	## Timeline editor
46	
47	Reference: Edge `pilot/sleep-editor-fixes` at `e0759a67f`, `lib/ui2/day_timeline/timeline_model.dart` and its shared timeline widgets. Implement in native Compose; do not import Flutter.
48	
49	Select a zone to edit its budget. Select a shared boundary before dragging it. Only the focused boundary is draggable; selection itself must not change time. Clamp movement to keep both adjacent zones at least 60 minutes. Fast dragging rounds to five-minute increments. Holding still for 600 ms activates one-minute increments at quarter-speed, anchored at the current value without a jump. Include zoom-in, zoom-out/reset, panning as needed, visible exact time, and accessible non-drag time controls. Full-day coverage never changes with zoom.
50	
51	Splitting defaults, chosen from the owner's examples:
52	
53	1. If focused duration is at least 120 minutes, divide its existing time into two valid windows, placing the new window after the focused one. Keep its outer boundaries.
54	2. Otherwise set focused and new windows to 60 minutes each. Borrow the deficit from the following adjacent window if it can retain 60 minutes, otherwise from the preceding adjacent window if it can retain 60 minutes. Exact 90 + 90 is valid. Never borrow across midnight or silently alter non-adjacent windows.
55	3. If neither adjacent neighbor suffices, make no change and show a modal instructing the user to enlarge the selected window or an adjacent window before splitting.
56	
57	Budget default for a new zone is zero; existing zones retain their numeric budgets. Reversible draft edits with Apply/Cancel avoid committing every pointer movement or triggering delivery on every drag frame. Apply uses last change wins and the common schedule write path. Removing a boundary merges its two zones; preserve total configured points and the active spend invariant. Do not change a running schedule during a partial drag.
58	
59	## Responsiveness and profiling
60	
61	Category browsing renders the cached catalog before refreshing discovery. Single-row edits must not rescan all apps or copy/rebuild the entire catalog. Avoid per-row binder/package lookups during composition and repeated icon decoding. Use stable lazy-list keys and lightweight collapsed rows; load expanded detail only when needed. Keep UI state writes on the UI dispatcher and prevent overlapping refreshes from clobbering more recent edits.
62	
63	Dashboard queries use bounded pages/ranges or SQL summaries; two collectors must not each materialize full unbounded history. Expanding a batch loads its items on demand. Do not delete history as a performance fix. Lifecycle-aware collection suspends unneeded UI work. Keep inbox filtering/paging consistent across active, cleared, priority, and search views.
64	
65	Add named trace sections/counters or an opt-in diagnostic view for discovery, list assembly, classification, database writes, delivery, retained action counts, and queue depth. Prefer existing platform tracing over a new telemetry backend. No title/text/reply data in instrumentation. Use `scripts/profile-notifications.py` for device memory/CPU/frame captures. Measured frame/energy claims require a real device capture, not source inspection.
66	
67	## Notification experiments
68	
69	Keep default proxy delivery working while exploring native timed snoozing. Android's public listener has timed snooze but no public arbitrary unsnooze. Do not bypass authorization using hidden APIs or pretend proxy posting restores source identity. Demonstrate handling updates, explicit source cancellation while snoozed, expiry, process restart, schedule changes, and budget exhaustion before enabling any native-original path. If exact budget control cannot be maintained, expose the experiment only in a controlled test path and explain the limitation in the pilot report.
70	
71	Source icons are a separate opt-in toggle. Prefer the original small icon where valid, retaining source app naming and actions, with a safe Farhan fallback. Mixed-provider summaries use Farhan's icon. Posting identity and channel ownership remain Farhan's unless the source explicitly delegates; icons do not imply delegated identity.
72	
73	## Verification and review
74	
75	Pilot tests cover these cases and production wiring. Include behavioral tests of the coordinator for cancellation/arrival/batch races and failed posting, per-app ordering under a priority boundary, budget-preserving schedule writes and intent replays, schedule split cases from the owner, minimum-width drag constraints, and automation validation. Tests must fail for plausible wrong implementations, with a WHY and catches comment. Do not pin source strings as behavioral proof. Avoid tests that only prove stubs or fixtures.
76	
77	Run a red phase before green and verify failures are assertions rather than missing symbols. Pure-domain stubs may be added for test compilation, but add no behavior in red. Focused tests/build checks run on one default-size Boat sandbox because this local host is a shared low-RAM ARM machine and the project Nix shell targets x86_64. Keep source caches warm and bring evidence back locally. Do not run a full repository sweep for this pilot.
78	
79	Review concerns default to durability 9/10 because this pilot stores data and delivers notifications, with error-paths, performance, architecture, and legibility at 6/10 unless the owner chooses higher bars. Serious correctness/security defects remain relevant regardless of concern score. Pilot build feedback is required before claiming the pilot accepted. No push or PR is authorized.
80	
81	## Defaults taken and open evidence
82	
83	- Neighbor order and no non-adjacent borrowing follow the examples and keep split changes local. If the owner wants searching farther away, revise explicitly.
84	- New zone budget zero avoids creating unrequested delivery allowance.
85	- Dated means a single local-date override; repeating is the fallback. Physiological sensors remain external.
86	- Automation authentication is opt-in to keep another installed app from silently changing the owner's interruption settings.
87	- Snoozing feasibility, source-icon rendering, retained-memory behavior, and scrolling require device/emulator evidence. Report unavailable verification honestly.

1	# Notification architecture review
2	
3	Reviewed `rework` at `8b7c2ec` on 2026-11-17. The owner's main use case is notification categorization, schedules, and budgets. The reported problems are accumulated background memory and slow category management. Visual changes are deferred to a later pilot.
4	
5	`origin/rework` has 9 commits absent from `main`, including the delivery pipeline and category registry. It lacks 45 commits present on `main`. Keep that divergence separate from performance changes so regressions remain attributable.
6	
7	## Findings
8	
9	These are source findings, not measured rankings of energy consumption. No device capture has been collected yet.
10	
11	| Concern | Evidence | Consequence to investigate |
12	| --- | --- | --- |
13	| Retained notification actions have no capacity or expiry | `NotificationService` holds process-wide `intentHashmap`, `actionsHashmap`, and `proxyToOriginalId`. `captureNotificationToInbox` retains tap and reply actions for both intercepted and pass-through notifications. `DeleteAllNotifications` only deletes database rows. | Memory can grow with retained notification keys; clearing the inbox does not release the corresponding actions. Individual deletion releases tap and reply actions through `ServiceUtilImpl`, but app cancellation and proxy removal mark rows cleared without doing that cleanup. |
14	| Category browsing waits for source discovery | `GetAppPriorityInfoList.invoke` runs installed and visible source scans before building the list. `ScanInstalledNotificationSources` enumerates installed apps and their channels, with a five-minute throttle. `buildInfo` checks notification status for each app. | Cold entry and entry after the throttle expires wait for package and notification-service calls. A priority edit calls `forPackage`, which copies the entire source registry through `getAll`, even though only one row changes. |
15	| Dashboard repeats full-history queries and transformations | `NotificationDashboardViewModel` separately observes summary and batches. Both use `repository.getNotifications()`, backed by `SELECT *`. Summary counts categories and priorities repeatedly; batches sorts and groups all records and retains item lists. | Every table invalidation can rematerialize and transform history twice. The debounce occurs after the repository's entity-to-domain mapping. Background dispatchers avoid blocking the UI directly but do not bound allocations or CPU work. |
16	| Notification processing has unbounded concurrency | `onNotificationPosted` launches a new IO coroutine for each event. Static action maps are ordinary `HashMap` objects accessed by service and UI paths. | Bursts can retain queued notification objects and perform concurrent mutations. Measure burst behavior and retained objects after work settles. |
17	| Budget spending is not serialized | `tryImmediateDelivery` and `deliverPendingNotifications` read, decide, post, and write the shared budget independently. The listener and delivery receiver can call them concurrently. | Two deliveries can authorize against the same balance and overwrite each other's spend. This is a correctness issue that should be fixed before increasing delivery throughput. |
18	| Registry persistence rewrites the entire registry | `KnownPackageSourceStore.register` serializes all known sources under a lock when a source changes. `processNotificationPosted` registers a source and then calls `getAll` to retrieve one package. | New channel/category discovery creates serialization and allocation work during notification arrival. Unchanged sources already avoid persistence; preserve that optimization. |
19	| Flood tracking retains individual timestamps | `PackageNotificationRateTracker` stores one timestamp per notification for an hour, prunes only the currently active package, and scans its deque on every record. | Memory and per-arrival work rise with burst size. Idle package entries retain old timestamps until that package posts again. |
20	
21	The notification listener on this branch already moves processing off its callback thread. The earlier `main` finding about blocking notification callbacks does not describe this branch. `SPEC_PERFORMANCE.md` predates parts of the notification rework and should not be treated as a complete description of the current implementation.
22	
23	## Proposed architecture
24	
25	Keep the existing pure classification resolver and `NotificationDeliveryPolicy`. Change the data flow and ownership around them.
26	
27	1. **Category browsing reads a local source catalog.** Render cached source rows immediately. Refresh discovery independently, publish changes, and invalidate on package/channel changes. Load channels when an app is expanded. A priority edit updates one row using a direct package lookup. Show whether discovery is running or failed without replacing usable cached content with a spinner.
28	2. **One delivery coordinator owns budget decisions.** Serialize immediate and scheduled delivery through the same coordinator. Persist notification state and budget reservations transactionally. Define crash recovery around the external notification-posting effect; a database transaction alone cannot make that effect atomic. Preserve critical and exempt pass-through behavior.
29	3. **Room serves summaries and bounded inbox pages.** Move counts and grouping into indexed queries with explicit time ranges. Load batch contents when expanded. Observe UI data only while needed. Keep active delivery work independent of dashboard collectors. Do not silently delete history to reduce memory.
30	4. **One action store owns transient notification actions.** Encapsulate synchronization and cleanup for tap intents, reply actions, and proxy mappings. Release entries on applicable deletion and clearing paths. Decide retention and fallback behavior before adding an eviction limit, since eviction affects whether old notifications remain actionable. PendingIntent objects cannot be restored from ordinary database records after process death.
31	5. **Diagnostics measure named operations.** Measure source discovery, category-list assembly, single-row edits, registry serialization, classification, inbox writes, budget authorization, and batch delivery. Count queue depth and retained action entries. Record durations and counts without notification titles, text, or reply content.
32	
33	Acceptance checks for the first implementation pass should include simultaneous arrivals against one remaining budget allocation, overlap with a scheduled batch, repeated category-screen entry, process restart, timezone and midnight changes, preserved critical pass-through, and memory after clearing a large inbox. Choose retention and crash-recovery behavior explicitly before changing those paths.
34	
35	## Profiling workflow
36	
37	`scripts/profile-notifications.py` captures device identity, installed package metadata, memory, CPU, battery statistics, services, jobs, and frame diagnostics. It does not reset statistics, force garbage collection, clear notifications, or change settings. It records command failures and timestamps in a manifest and exits nonzero for incomplete captures. Diagnostic text may still report permission or OEM limitations with a zero shell exit code; inspect the files before drawing conclusions.
38	
39	Run inside the Nix development environment with a connected, authorized phone:
40	
41	```bash
42	nix develop -c python3 scripts/profile-notifications.py categories-before --note 'Installed build; enabled features; inbox size; device state'
43	# Open category management, expand several apps, and edit one priority.
44	nix develop -c python3 scripts/profile-notifications.py categories-after --note 'Time to first usable list; edits; visible pauses'
45	```
46	
47	Use `--serial DEVICE` if multiple devices are attached. Captures go into the already ignored `captures/notifications` directory. They can contain package names and device details; review before sharing.
48	
49	Repeat the following scenarios on the same build and device, noting workload size, screen brightness, enabled features, charging state, and thermal conditions:
50	
51	- Idle with the screen off, before and after a fixed observation period.
52	- Category management after process launch, repeated entry, and entry after five minutes.
53	- Controlled notification bursts using the existing `testing/` demo apps. Capture before the burst, after processing settles, and after clearing the inbox.
54	- Arrival overlapping a scheduled delivery boundary with a nearly exhausted budget.
55	
56	Use Android Studio's memory profiler to inspect retained objects after repeated bursts and clearing. A memory snapshot alone cannot establish a leak or its battery impact. Record a System Trace while reproducing category latency to distinguish package-service waits, allocations, scheduling, and rendering. Compare equivalent before/after workloads; do not infer precise energy savings from RAM size or battery percentage alone.
57	
58	Official references: [dumpsys diagnostics](https://developer.android.com/tools/dumpsys), [wake-lock diagnostics and system tracing](https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/background-tasks/awake/wakelock/debug-locally), [battery profiling guidance](https://developer.android.com/topic/performance/power/setup-battery-historian). Android's guidance now favors system tracing, Macrobenchmark power metrics, or Power Profiler over the unmaintained Battery Historian workflow.
